passage:
I'm Ritu. I sat in the third row of assembly the day Rajni gave the talk on our school's water problem.
When she walked up, her index cards were shaking so much I could hear them. For the first few seconds she looked only at the floor. Then she did something odd: she stopped, took a breath, and looked straight at the back wall, above everyone's heads.
She started with a question: "How many of you found the second-floor tap dry today?" Hands went up. People laughed. After that she had us.
She had three points, one per card, and she ended with a small ask: report leaks on the chart outside the staffroom.
Her voice still wobbled on the last line. I can't say if she was still scared. But she didn't rush.

qa.q: How did Rajni start her talk?
qa.a: She started with a question: "How many of you found the second-floor tap dry today?"

qa.q: What do Rajni's shaking cards suggest about how she felt at first?
qa.a: They suggest Rajni was very nervous and afraid of the audience when she walked up.

qa.q: Which of Rajni's choices helped her hold the audience, and why?
qa.a: Opening with a question about something everyone had experienced made people laugh and pay attention, and three simple points kept it clear.

qa.q: How might the students in the hall have seen Rajni's talk?
qa.a: They probably felt included and interested, because the question was about their own day, so they listened rather than judged her nerves.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a teen managing stage fear and holding an audience with a clear structure.

passage:
Monday. Hafsa practised her science fair talk on her friend Maria in the library corner. It went everywhere: solar ovens, her cousin in Rajasthan, a video she'd seen. After four minutes, Maria asked, "Wait, what's the point?" Hafsa groaned and put her head on the desk.
Wednesday. Maria helped her cut it down to three parts: the problem, how her oven works, what she measured. One sentence each on a card. Hafsa practised in front of the mirror, then in front of her little brother, who kept yawning on purpose.
Friday, the fair. Halfway through, a judge asked a question and Hafsa's mind went blank. She glanced at card two, took a breath and said, "Let me come back to that." She finished, then answered it properly.
Maria gave her a thumbs up from behind the judges.

qa.q: What three parts did Maria help Hafsa cut the talk into?
qa.a: The problem, how her oven works, and what she measured.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling on Monday when she put her head on the desk?
qa.a: Hafsa felt frustrated and discouraged, because her talk had rambled and Maria couldn't find the point.

qa.q: What could someone with a blank mind on stage learn from Hafsa's Friday?
qa.a: Keep a simple card for each part, glance at it, breathe, and say you'll come back to a question rather than panicking.

qa.q: How might Maria feel watching Hafsa recover in front of the judges?
qa.a: Maria probably feels proud and relieved, since Maria helped build the structure that saved the moment.

grounding: Illustrates, over several days, a teen structuring a talk and handling a moment of stage fear.

passage:
Pradeep, before you go up to speak at that conference, let me tell you about my first speech.
I was fifteen. Our school's annual day. I had learned four pages by heart. I walked up, saw six hundred faces and my mind went white. I stood there. Somebody coughed. I could hear the fans.
Then Mr Joseph, our English teacher, walked to the side of the stage and held up a card he'd made me write: "Why I love trains." Just that. I'd told him the whole speech was about my grandfather's railway job.
So I dropped the pages and told them about the night mail and my grandfather's lantern. Five minutes. People clapped properly.
Since then I never learn speeches by heart. I learn the story. That's what your Rafiq Chacha knows.

qa.q: What did Mr Joseph hold up at the side of the stage?
qa.a: He held up a card that said "Why I love trains."

qa.q: How did young Rafiq feel when his mind went white?
qa.a: Young Rafiq felt frozen with fear, standing silent in front of six hundred faces.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Dropping the memorised pages to tell the real story of his grandfather worked, because he was speaking from memory and feeling instead of recitation.

qa.q: How might Mr Joseph have felt standing at the side of the stage?
qa.a: Mr Joseph was probably anxious for his student and then relieved and proud when the card helped him recover.

grounding: Shows an elder recounting how, as a teen, he overcame stage fear by telling a story rather than reciting.

passage:
You asked on the school podcast why I deleted the video app. Okay. I'm Damini, and honestly I didn't delete it at first. I just noticed something weird.
I'd open it for one dance video before homework. Then another one would start by itself. Then it showed me stuff I didn't even search for, but somehow exactly what I'd watch. One night I looked up and it was 1 a.m. and my maths was still open.
My friend Saurabh said, "It's not you. It's built like that. Autoplay, endless scroll, the little red dots. They want your time." He showed me where to switch off autoplay and notifications.
It felt like finding the trick behind a magic show. I was kind of angry, actually. Now I set a timer, and when it rings I close it. Most days.

qa.q: What did Saurabh show Damini how to switch off?
qa.a: He showed Damini where to switch off autoplay and notifications.

qa.q: How did Damini feel after learning how the app was built?
qa.a: Damini felt angry, like finding the trick behind a magic show, realising the app was designed to take up time.

qa.q: What else could Damini try if the timer stops working?
qa.a: Damini could keep the app off the home screen, use it only after homework, or ask a friend to check in on the plan.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Damini's change?
qa.a: Saurabh might feel glad that telling the truth about the design helped, rather than blaming Damini for being weak.

grounding: Illustrates a teen realising that autoplay, endless feeds and notifications are designed to hold attention.

passage:
I'm Yamini, Anirban's older sister, and I watched this happen over a month.
Anirban liked one video about building muscle. Just one. By the next week his whole feed was shirtless guys, protein shakes and "you're lazy if you don't train twice a day". He started looking at himself in the mirror a lot, and he got quiet at dinner.
One evening I sat next to him and asked what he was watching. He scrolled and scrolled, and it was all the same thing.
He said, slowly, "I never asked for all this."
So he tried a test: he searched for cooking and birds for three days and hit "not interested" on the gym videos. The feed changed. I can't say exactly what he felt, but he started laughing at dinner again.

qa.q: What kind of videos did Anirban's feed fill with?
qa.a: Shirtless guys, protein shakes and "you're lazy if you don't train twice a day".

qa.q: What does Anirban's "I never asked for all this" suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Anirban felt surprised and uneasy, realising the feed had pushed far more at him than he chose.

qa.q: What small step helped Anirban take back some control?
qa.a: Searching other topics and marking the gym videos "not interested" retrained the feed, which showed it could be changed.

qa.q: Why might Yamini be careful about saying what Anirban felt?
qa.a: Yamini is watching from outside, so she can see him get quiet or laugh but can't know his thoughts for sure.

grounding: Shows, through a sibling's eyes, a teen discovering how one click shapes a recommendation feed.

passage:
Sunday: Farhan posted a photo from the cricket ground and checked it every few minutes. Twelve likes. Then fourteen. He refreshed during dinner. When Tejas liked it late, Farhan texted, "Finally."
Tuesday: Tejas came over with a printout from his computer class about how apps are designed: likes that arrive in bursts, streaks you lose if you skip a day, notifications timed for when you're bored. "It's like a slot machine," Tejas said. Farhan laughed, then stopped laughing.
Thursday: Farhan hid like counts in the settings and turned off notifications after 9 p.m. He was twitchy the first evening, reaching for the phone. By the second evening he'd finished a book chapter.
"You didn't reply to my streak," Tejas texted on Friday.
"Yeah," Farhan wrote back. "I'm out of the casino."

qa.q: What did Farhan turn off after 9 p.m.?
qa.a: Farhan turned off notifications after 9 p.m.

qa.q: Why did Farhan stop laughing at Tejas's slot machine comparison?
qa.a: Farhan felt uncomfortable and a bit uneasy, recognising his own habit of refreshing for likes in it.

qa.q: Which change helped Farhan most, and why?
qa.a: Hiding like counts and switching off late notifications helped, because it removed the triggers that kept pulling him back.

qa.q: How does Tejas see the change when Farhan misses the streak?
qa.a: Tejas seems to accept it with some amusement, since he was the one who explained how streaks are designed.

grounding: Illustrates over several days a teen understanding how likes, streaks and notifications are built to keep users hooked, and setting limits.

passage:
When I was thirteen I posted a meme about our maths teacher's handwriting. Just a photo of the board with a joke caption. Forty people laughed at it. I felt clever.
I deleted it a week later, when I got bored of it. I thought that was the end.
Two years later I stood for class prefect. The evening before the vote, Jyoti forwarded me a screenshot. Someone had saved it. It was going round the class group with "Is THIS our prefect?"
My stomach dropped. I couldn't delete a screenshot.
So I didn't try to hide. I went to Sir and apologised, properly. Then, in my speech, I said, "Some of you have seen my old post. It was unkind and I'm sorry. I'm Bidisha, and I'm not that person now."
I lost by six votes. But Sir smiles at me now.

qa.q: What did the class group caption on the screenshot say?
qa.a: "Is THIS our prefect?"

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when Jyoti forwarded the screenshot?
qa.a: Bidisha felt shocked and ashamed, and the passage says Bidisha's stomach dropped.

qa.q: What went right in how Bidisha handled the old post, and what could have prevented it?
qa.a: Owning it and apologising to Sir and the class was honest; thinking before posting about a real person would have prevented it.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when Bidisha came to apologise?
qa.a: Sir may have felt hurt by the old joke but touched and respected that Bidisha came to say sorry directly.

grounding: Shows a teen discovering that a deleted post persisted and shaped reputation years later.

passage:
Counsellor's note, 15 November. Binita (school counsellor).
Anirban came to me worried. He has a state football trial next month and a friend told him selectors "check your profile". He was scrolling through three years of posts, deleting in a panic.
We went through them together, calmly. Most were fine: matches, his dog. A few needed thought: a video of him and friends mocking another team, a comment calling a referee "blind". He went red reading those. He said, "I didn't think anyone would ever see it again."
We talked about what the posts say about him to a stranger. He deleted the mocking video, and he messaged the other team's captain to apologise. The comment was on someone else's page; he asked them to remove it.
Plan: he'll think "Would I say this to their face?" before posting. I'll check in after the trial.

qa.q: What did a friend tell Anirban about the selectors?
qa.a: A friend told him selectors "check your profile".

qa.q: Why did Anirban go red reading the video and the referee comment?
qa.a: Anirban felt embarrassed and ashamed, because he hadn't expected those posts to be seen again, and they showed him mocking people.

qa.q: What would you advise a teen in Anirban's place?
qa.a: Review posts calmly, remove what is unkind, apologise where someone was hurt, and think "Would I say this to their face?" before posting.

qa.q: How might the other team's captain see Anirban's apology?
qa.a: The captain might be surprised and feel respected, seeing that the mocking was taken seriously even years later.

grounding: Illustrates a counsellor helping a teen see that old posts persist and shape how strangers judge him.

passage:
Saturday night
Diary, Saurabh here. Arohi's birthday party was fun until she said, "Post the group pic!"
In the best photo, Ved is mid-sneeze. Honestly it's hilarious. Everyone wanted it up. But I kept thinking: in a year, someone will screenshot it and make stickers, like they did to Priyanshu last year. Ved still gets called "Tomato Face" from that.
So I texted Ved: "Can I post the sneeze one?" He wrote back, "PLEASE don't."
Arohi was annoyed. "You're so serious." We posted the other one where everyone's normal. Nobody died.
Later Ved sent me a thank-you meme, privately. It's weird how one photo can follow you around. I think I'm going to go through my own old posts this weekend.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh hesitate to post the sneeze photo?
qa.a: Saurabh felt uneasy and worried that it could be screenshotted and follow Ved around, like Priyanshu's photo did.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Ved before posting worked, because the person in the photo got to decide about their own image.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Saurabh's choice later?
qa.a: Arohi was annoyed at the party, but later she might see that Saurabh protected a friend without spoiling her birthday.

passage:
Last term I had a history essay due on the old trade routes, and I was lazy. I typed the question into an AI chatbot and got a perfect-looking answer, with three book references at the bottom. I nearly handed it in.
Ankita, my project partner, said, "Let's get one of those books from the library for pictures." The librarian searched for twenty minutes. The book didn't exist. Neither did the second one.
I felt sick. I'd almost submitted fake sources with my name on them.
So we started again. I used the chatbot to explain things I didn't get, like what a monsoon trade wind actually does, then checked each idea in our textbook and one real book. I wrote it myself.
Got a B. My name's Eshaan and it was the first B I actually earned.

qa.q: What did the librarian find when searching for the books?
qa.a: The book didn't exist, and neither did the second one.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel on learning the references were fake?
qa.a: Eshaan felt sick and alarmed at having almost submitted fake sources under Eshaan's own name.

qa.q: What would you advise someone using AI for homework after this?
qa.a: Use it to explain ideas, then check every claim and reference in real sources, and write the work yourself.

qa.q: How might Ankita see the project after the library search?
qa.a: Ankita probably felt relieved the fake sources were caught and more confident in the rewritten version they checked together.

grounding: Illustrates a teen discovering an AI tool invented citations and switching to using it for understanding plus verification.

Biology teacher's note, Class 10B (Sunaina Ma'am)
I told the class they could use AI tools to understand topics, as long as they wrote their answers themselves and checked the facts.
Zeenat showed me something interesting today. She had asked a chatbot to explain photosynthesis in simple steps. It was helpful, but it said plants give out oxygen "only at night". She frowned at that, checked her textbook and our lab notes, and found it was wrong.
She wrote her own explanation, then put a small note at the bottom: "AI helped explain steps; night claim was wrong, corrected from textbook, p. 84."
I asked her permission and shared her note with the class as an example. Next week I'm going to give everyone an AI answer with two hidden errors to find.

qa.q: What wrong claim did the chatbot make?
qa.a: It said plants give out oxygen "only at night".

qa.q: What does Zeenat's frown at the night claim suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Zeenat felt doubtful and suspicious, sensing the claim didn't fit what she already knew.

qa.q: How could Sunaina Ma'am's error-hunting task help the class?
qa.a: It would train everyone to treat AI answers as drafts to check, not facts to copy.

qa.q: How might Zeenat's classmates see her note when it's shared?
qa.a: They might feel surprised that an AI can be confidently wrong and realise checking is part of using it honestly.

grounding: Shows a teacher noting a teen using AI to learn while checking and correcting its claims.

passage:
Thursday
It's 11 pm and Bhupen here, too tired for maths. I opened the AI app and was about to type "solve all of exercise 6.3". Deepika Didi walked past and said, "If you do that, you'll be stuck in the exam, when there's no app."
Annoying but true.
So I only asked it to explain question 4, which I didn't get. It explained the method. Then I did 5 to 8 myself. For question 7, I got a different answer from what it gave when I checked. I did it three times. I was right; it had made a sign mistake.
That felt amazing, honestly. Like catching a teacher out.
Tomorrow I'll ask Sir if my method for 7 is right, just to be sure.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel on finding the AI's sign mistake?
qa.a: Bhupen felt amazed and proud, like catching a teacher out.

qa.q: What was wise about checking with Sir tomorrow?
qa.a: It adds a real person's check, so Bhupen doesn't swap trusting the AI for blindly trusting a single recalculation.

qa.q: How does Deepika Didi see using the app for the whole exercise?
qa.a: Deepika Didi sees it as a trap, because the app won't be there in the exam and Bhupen wouldn't have learned anything.

passage:
During the hostel's evening computer hour, Hrithik got a message on the class email: "Congratulations! You've won a new phone. Pay a small delivery fee and enter your bank OTP to claim." There was a countdown: 15 minutes left.
Hrithik was already reaching for his father's bank details on a note in his wallet. "It's from a real company, look at the logo."
Vijay leaned over. "Why would a free phone need an OTP? And the email address is a mix of numbers."
Hrithik hesitated. "But the timer…"
"The timer is the trick. So you don't think."
They took it to Mr Pinto, the lab in-charge, before doing anything. He checked it, said it was a scam, reported it to the school's IT team that evening and warned the whole hostel at dinner. He also called Hrithik's father, who hid the card details safely.

qa.q: What did the message ask Hrithik to enter to claim the phone?
qa.a: It asked him to pay a small delivery fee and enter his bank OTP.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he reached for the bank details?
qa.a: Hrithik felt excited and rushed by the countdown, and trusted the logo.

qa.q: Which clues did Vijay spot, and why is taking it to an adult the right step?
qa.a: Vijay spotted that a free phone doesn't need an OTP, and the odd email address; an adult could confirm the scam and report it quickly.

qa.q: How might Hrithik's father feel when Mr Pinto calls?
qa.a: His father might feel shaken that the card details were nearly shared, but relieved and grateful the boys asked for help first.

grounding: Shows teens recognising a fraud message's pressure tactics and reporting it to a trusted adult.

passage:
Dear Jaya Chechi,
Remember when you told me that anyone online who asks you to keep secrets is not a friend? I need to tell you that it helped.
There was a guy in my online game who said he was sixteen. He gave me free items for weeks. Then he started asking for photos, and said, "Don't tell your parents, they won't get it." My stomach went cold when I read that. It was exactly what you said.
I didn't reply. I took screenshots, blocked him, and went to Appa straight away, even though it was late. He didn't get angry. He said I did the right thing, sat with me while we reported the account to the game, and filled in the cyber crime report online that same night. This morning he told my class teacher too.
I feel stupid for trusting him. Appa says I shouldn't.
Jomon

qa.q: What did the player say when asking for photos?
qa.a: He said, "Don't tell your parents, they won't get it."

qa.q: How did Jomon feel on reading the request for secrecy?
qa.a: Jomon felt a cold jolt of fear, recognising the warning sign Jaya Chechi had described.

qa.q: What did Jomon do that others could follow?
qa.a: Jomon didn't reply, took screenshots, blocked the account and told a trusted adult straight away, who reported it that night.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when Jomon came to him late at night?
qa.a: Appa was probably alarmed but proud and relieved that Jomon told him, which is why he stayed calm and acted at once. 🤍

passage:
You asked how I dealt with it, so I'll say it straight. My name's Ramesh. Last year, someone I'd chatted with on a forum sent me an edited photo, my face stuck on something awful, and said, "Pay, or I send this to your whole school."
I couldn't breathe properly. I thought about paying. I thought about disappearing.
Instead I called my uncle Shankar. He's the one who never shouts. He came over that same hour. First thing he said: "This is not your fault, and you are not paying anyone." We didn't reply to the message. We saved everything, blocked the account and filed a complaint on the national cyber crime portal. The next morning he came with me to my principal.
The photo never went out. Maybe it would have, maybe not. But telling someone that day made it stop being mine to carry alone.

qa.q: What did Uncle Shankar say first?
qa.a: "This is not your fault, and you are not paying anyone."

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when the threat arrived?
qa.a: Ramesh felt terrified and trapped, struggling to breathe and thinking about paying or disappearing.

qa.q: Which steps did Ramesh and Shankar take, and why do they matter?
qa.a: They didn't reply, saved the evidence, blocked the account, reported it to the cyber crime portal and told the principal, so the blackmailer lost power and adults could act.

qa.q: How might Uncle Shankar have felt when Ramesh called him?
qa.a: Shankar was probably worried and angry at the blackmailer, but calm on the outside so Ramesh would feel safe.

grounding: Shows a teen facing a blackmail attempt, telling a trusted adult the same day and reporting it.

passage:
In Kalimpong, Tenzin's family had one smartphone, and after dinner it was his. He played a football game on it until the battery died, usually after midnight.
One morning at the bus stand, Hafsa had to shake him awake. At school he fell asleep on his arms during history, and Madam asked him to wash his face. His cheeks burned.
That evening he watched himself. He picked up the phone at 8 for "two matches". At 11 his mother said, "Tenzin, the whole house is asleep." He hadn't noticed the time at all.
He felt a bit scared by that. So he made a rule and told his mother about it: the phone charges in the kitchen at 10, with her. The first night he lay awake, itchy. By the fourth night he was asleep before the dogs started barking.

passage:
Astrid lived in Tromsø, where in December the sun didn't come up at all. That made it easy to lose track of time. She'd get into bed at ten with the video app and look up at two.
One Monday, her friend Tuan said, "You look like a ghost." She laughed but felt awful. She checked her phone's screen report: almost four hours after 10 p.m., every night.
She tried an experiment. For one week, the phone stayed on her desk across the room, with an alarm clock instead. She read a paper book in bed, even though the first nights she kept reaching for the bedside table out of habit.
On Friday she noticed she'd answered three questions in maths. Tuan noticed too. "Who are you?"
"Someone who sleeps," Astrid said.

qa.q: How long did Astrid's phone report show after 10 p.m.?
qa.a: Almost four hours after 10 p.m., every night.

qa.q: How did Astrid feel when Tuan said she looked like a ghost?
qa.a: She laughed but felt awful, worried about how tired she had become.

qa.q: Which part of Astrid's experiment helped most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the phone across the room with an alarm clock helped, because the phone wasn't within reach when the habit kicked in.

qa.q: How might Tuan see Astrid on Friday?
qa.a: Tuan seems surprised and pleased, joking "Who are you?" because she is suddenly awake and answering in class.

grounding: Illustrates a teen using a screen-time report to notice compulsive night scrolling and setting a limit.

passage:
After the wedding season in their small town, Zeenat started comparing herself to a video star whose skin and waist looked perfect in every clip. She began leaving half her lunch, saying she wasn't hungry.
Her cousin Farida, a year older, noticed. One afternoon on the roof, she showed Zeenat a trick: the same photo of herself, with and without a filter. "See? Smoother skin, thinner face. It's the app, not me."
Zeenat laughed a little, then went quiet. "But she's like that in every video."
"Every video has the filter," Farida said. "And you're growing. Growing needs food."
That night Farida sat with Zeenat while she told Ammi about the lunches. Ammi didn't scold. She hugged her, and said they'd see the doctor together if Zeenat kept feeling bad about eating.

qa.q: What did Farida show Zeenat on the roof?
qa.a: The same photo of herself, with and without a filter.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat go quiet after laughing?
qa.a: Zeenat still felt insecure and doubtful, comparing herself to the star who looked perfect in every video.

qa.q: What was the most important step Farida took, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with Zeenat while she told Ammi mattered most, because skipping food is a real problem that needs a trusted adult involved.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt hearing about the lunches?
qa.a: Ammi was probably worried but chose to be calm and loving, so Zeenat would keep talking to her.

grounding: Shows a teen affected by idealised filtered images starting to skip food, and family helping her toward self-acceptance and adult support.

passage:
In Brno, the swim class changing room was where Jana felt worst. Her body had changed fast over the summer, and she kept her towel wrapped round her even while changing. She was sure everyone was looking.
One Wednesday, Sofia, from the next bench, said quietly, "I hate this room too. I change in the toilet cubicle sometimes."
Jana stared. Sofia was the fastest swimmer in the group.
"Seriously?"
"Everyone's weird about their body right now. We're all changing."
Jana thought about that in the water. Her legs were strong; her times were good. The coach said her turns were the best in the class.
It didn't disappear. But the next week she didn't wrap the towel quite so tight, and she and Sofia raced the last length laughing.

qa.q: Where does Sofia sometimes change?
qa.a: Sofia sometimes changes in the toilet cubicle.

qa.q: Why did Jana stare when Sofia admitted hating the room too?
qa.a: Jana felt surprised, and a bit relieved, because she had assumed only she felt self-conscious.

qa.q: How could the coach help students who feel like Jana?
qa.a: The coach could offer private changing spaces and praise what bodies can do, like strong legs and good turns, not how they look.

At the sports hostel, Trisha's arms had grown strong from two years of wrestling. One evening in the mess, a few boys from the hockey team flexed and called her "Bhim". Everyone laughed.

In their small town near the river, Chinmay came home from tuition and slammed the door so hard the calendar fell. His sister Shreya, doing homework on the floor, looked up.
"What happened?"
"Nothing! Why does everyone keep asking?"
She went back to her book. He stood in the middle of the room, breathing hard. Nothing had happened. That was the strange part. He just felt like everything was too loud and too close.
He grabbed his cycle and rode to the ghat. He sat watching the boats for twenty minutes until his chest stopped feeling tight.

She shrugged. "You were like a pressure cooker."
